questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $B=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find ${e}^{B}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and the given matrix $B,$ we have

$$
{e}^{B}={e}^{PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $3$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)={e}^{x}.$ So, we get

$$
{e}^{J}=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 1-3\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{B} & =P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & -2{e}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3} & -4{e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & -{e}^{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${e}^{{J}_{3}(1)}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)={e}^{x},$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =1.$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2!} \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}e & e & \frac{e}{2} \\ 0 & e & e \\ 0 & 0 & e\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =2.$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(2) \\ 0 & f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{8} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $X=PD{P}^{-1},$ find ${X}^{5}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={x}^{5}$ and the given matrix $X,$ we have

$$
{X}^{5}=(PD{P}^{-1})^{5}=P\cdot ({D}^{5})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
{D}^{5}=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{5} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 32\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{2}{2\cdot 1-3\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{5} & =P\cdot ({D}^{5})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 32\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -96 & 64\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-92 & 62 \\ -186 & 125\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{([\begin{aligned}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(0)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(3),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\ .\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(0),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(0)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(0) & {f}^{′}(0) & \frac{{f}^{″}(0)}{2} \\ 0 & f(0) & {f}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & 0 & f(0)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{0} & {e}^{0} & \frac{{e}^{0}}{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{0} & {e}^{0} \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{0}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
